author: Cree Say
title: A SYMPHONY OF SECRETS The sins we hide series Book 4
text: put,” he instructed, and I nodded, though trembling inside. I could feel my pulse in my temples. Panic clawed through me, hot and suffocating. Images of Ray being recognized flooded my mind: toddlers pointed at on playgrounds, strangers whispering, fans posting every photo online. I felt like I’d been exposed, raw and bleeding, in front of the world I’d tried to keep at bay for two years. Every instinct screamed at me to protect her, to shield her from this spotlight, but there was no hiding anymore. Amy finally dropped her phone, breathing heavily, but still working through contacts, speaking rapidly. “I’ve got the legal team ready. Jordan, your connections,push them now. We need takedown notices and media control immediately. Lys, stay with the kids, do not move until I say so.” I nodded numbly, gripping Ray tightly as she buried her face into my chest, tiny tears soaking into my sweater. Emeric stirred but didn’t wake fully, lulled by Amy’s calm presence. I felt utterly helpless, and the guilt was immediate and crushing. Isaiah. Oh God, Isaiah. I pictured him seeing this chaos, seeing my child, the world dissecting our lives while he was left out,or worse, thinking I had betrayed something sacred in keeping Ray hidden from him. My fingers twitched helplessly as if I could claw back the images. Jordan crouched beside me again, his strong presence radiating calm in a room that had gone mad. He pressed a finger to my lips, firm yet gentle. “Lys, listen. None of this changes who you are or who she is. We contain this now, together. I’ve got this. Amy has this. You have us. That’s all that matters.” I leaned against him, shuddering, heart hammering violently in my chest. His scent, that intoxicating mix of leather and wood and something uniquely Jordan, grounded me. Desire mingled with fear, and for a moment, I wanted to escape the chaos by clinging to him, by letting every rational thought dissolve into the warmth of his arms. The children, sensing tension but too young to understand its gravity, clung to us both. Ray’s tiny fingers kneaded into my shirt, and I whispered, “It’s okay, princess. Mama’s here. You’re safe.” Emeric stirred again, letting out a little sigh, and Amy smoothed his hair back with a practiced hand. The chaos outside seemed momentarily distant, swallowed by the need to protect these tiny, perfect lives. Jordan leaned in, his lips brushing the top of my head, and whispered against my hair, “You did nothing wrong. You are not the story. The world doesn’t get to touch her. Not now. Not ever.” I closed my eyes, letting his words wash over me, but panic clawed at the edges. My mind spun with images of headlines, of comments speculating about Ray’s father, about me being a mother in hiding. I could feel the eyes of the world pressing through every wall, through every shuttered window, into our home, into our lives. Amy’s phone rang, shrill and urgent. She answered quickly, nodding and speaking in rapid bursts. “Yes… yes… take it down… immediately… flag the post… contact your manager… we need every editor on standby… yes, I understand…” She hung up and turned to us, eyes blazing with controlled fury. “We’ve slowed it. Not fully contained, but slowed. We need to get you all inside, secured, now. Jordan, make sure you lock this down.” Jordan rose, placing one last reassuring hand on my shoulder. “Come on,” he said, and we moved toward the inner apartment, Ray pressed tightly against me. Each flash outside felt like knives slicing through my chest. Every phone recording felt like betrayal. Once inside, doors locked, blinds drawn, I finally allowed myself to sink into the sofa, Ray curled against my side, Emeric still asleep on Amy’s shoulder. The adrenaline that had kept me upright melted, leaving only raw, trembling exhaustion. Tears rolled down my cheeks freely, unrestrained. Jordan knelt beside me, brushing wet strands of hair from my face. “You’re safe now,” he said quietly. “We’ve got this under control. Nothing can touch you or her inside these walls.” I clutched Ray to me, feeling the guilt and panic still swirling inside. “It’s everywhere,” I whispered. “It’s online. People… they’ve already seen her face. They’ll know… they’ll figure out who she is. What if Isaiah… what if…” My voice faltered entirely. Jordan tipped my chin up, forcing my gaze to meet his. “None of that matters right now. We can control this. We will control this. Amy’s working magic, I’m using my contacts, and you,stay with Ray. You keep her safe. That’s your job. The rest is mine.” I let myself cling to him, heart racing, body trembling. Desire, fear, guilt, and relief tangled together. I wanted to kiss him, to anchor myself to him in the only way that felt real amid the chaos. And when I did, his lips met mine with a heat that drew out all the fear, if only momentarily, replacing it with urgency, need, and a strange, grounding comfort. The storm outside still raged, but inside these walls, Jordan’s presence, Amy’s fierce competence, and Ray’s innocent sleep created a bubble of fragile calm. And yet, I couldn’t shake the gnawing fear that Isaiah might already know, that the world would continue to intrude, that the fragile bubble could shatter in the next moment. I pressed my lips to Jordan’s again, needing the only safety I could control: him, his warmth, his certainty. In that moment, amidst chaos, panic, and media frenzy, I realized something terrifying and liberating: the world could expose me, they could dissect me, they could scream my secrets into the void,but in this room, in his arms, I could still breathe. And for the first time tonight, I let myself do just that. Twenty Nine Isaiah I puked all my gut into the bowl again, groaning as the acidic taste burned the back of my throat. I just wanted everything to end. One peaceful moment, one second of quiet, seemed impossible. The chemo days were hellish, a war my body fought without mercy, leaving me battered and raw. “Drink the water,” Leo said softly, holding the bottle out to me. I opened my mouth to give him a crude remark, but before a word could leave my lips, another wave of nausea hit, and I vomited again into the bowl. My throat burned from the acid, my chest tightened, and every muscle in my body screamed. Painkillers did little to dull the torment. I hate this. I hate cancer. I hate chemo. I hate the helplessness that accompanies every breath. I hate feeling my body betray me, turning against me in ways I cannot control. My lungs, once strong, wheezed with every shallow intake of air. My legs felt like lead. My skin, clammy and pale, was slick with sweat. I could feel my nerves fraying, my composure slipping in thin, ragged strips. “There is blood—is it normal?” Julian’s voice came, muffled yet insistent. “Yes. There is nothing wrong; he’ll be okay,” the nurse replied, calm and professional. I waited, lying on the sterile hospital sheets, stomach churning, hoping the nausea would finally subside. After five minutes of relative quiet, I handed the bowl to the nurse for disposal and leaned back, letting the bed cradle my trembling body. Pain radiated through me like a constant electric current, and the only relief came from the brief pause between nausea waves. I could feel the disease inside me, gnawing relentlessly. I had known this day would come, but knowing it didn’t make it any easier. Finally, I exhaled slowly, letting my mind wander to the unspoken truths I’d been avoiding for months. Parkinson’s disease. A rare, aggressive form of lung cancer,small-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma,that had spread to my brain. The doctors had been honest, brutal in their words: there was no cure. None. Only aggressive chemotherapy, experimental treatments, and a hope so thin it felt like holding onto smoke. I hated being honest about it, even to myself. I hated the vulnerability. But I couldn’t hide it anymore. Not from the sterile lights, not from the cold hospital walls, and certainly not from my own consciousness, which refused to let me pretend. I thought about the tremors, the stiffness, the way my body had started betraying me long before the diagnosis became official. I thought about the cancer cells that didn’t respect my plans or my history, the ones now inching into my brain, rewriting the rules of my life without permission. The chemotherapy might slow it,maybe,but there were no guarantees. No promises. I let myself feel it now. The fear. The exhaustion. The sorrow. The rage. All of it swirled inside me, heavy and suffocating. An hour later, I woke from a brief nap, restless and still nauseated, though the worst of it had passed. My phone lay beside me, screen lit, Netflix paused mid-scene. I scrolled absentmindedly, trying to distract myself. There was nothing else to do. I couldn’t walk far; every movement left my breath ragged, shallow, desperate. The oxygen machine hissed softly beside my bed, a lifeline I had come to rely on in a way I hated. The quiet was broken when Leo entered the room. His eyes widened slightly, a mixture of surprise and urgency etched on his face. “Isaiah… you need to see this,” he said, holding his phone like it was a detonator. My chest tightened instinctively, the premonition twisting in my gut. “What is it?” I croaked, voice hoarse, throat raw. He gestured for me to focus on the screen. I did, even though my mind fought, even though every instinct screamed to hide. The headlines blurred at first: Alyssa Spotted with Mystery Baby Who’s the Father? Alyssa’s Daughter Revealed, Speculation Explodes Online. Screenshots of tweets and Instagram posts flooded my vision. Comments, thousands of them, rolled in at a speed I couldn’t comprehend. People were speculating, pointing fingers, twisting the story in every direction. My heart stopped when I saw the photograph. My breath hitched painfully, like someone had reached into my chest and squeezed everything tight. There she was. A little girl,tiny, maybe two years old,with wild brown curls and eyes so green they practically glowed from the screen. She was perched on Alyssa’s hip, her small hand gripping Alyssa’s blouse, her round cheeks flushed as she squinted at the camera. I didn’t know her name. I didn’t know anything about her. I hadn’t even known Alyssa was pregnant. But the second I looked at her… something in me fractured. Those eyes. God,those eyes. My lungs forgot how to work. My fingers twitched violently. I leaned forward as if getting closer would change the reality staring me in the face. The shape of her eyes, the soft curl of her lashes, the exact shade of bright, startling green. It was me. She looked like me. Down to the little crease at the corner of her left eye. Down to the same stubborn, determined stare I’ve had all my life. I didn’t need a DNA test. Not for this. Not for her. Some truths lived in the blood. Some truths punched you straight in the soul the moment you saw them. This one did. My hands shook so hard I had to grip the blanket. My voice barely crawled out of my chest. “Leo…” He didn’t answer at first. He was staring just as hard, jaw clenched, eyes wide with disbelief. “Holy shit,” he whispered. “Isaiah.” I swallowed, or tried to. My throat felt scraped raw. “Alyssa… has a child?” “She never announced anything,” Leo murmured. “There were no pictures, no rumors, nothing for the past two years. But—” His eyes flicked to me again. “Man… she looks like you.” My stomach twisted, churned, collapsed in on itself. My chest trembled under the weight of something too big to name. “I… I didn’t know,” I whispered. My voice cracked in the middle, thin and broken. “I didn’t even know she was pregnant.” The guilt hit next,sharp, catastrophic. A tidal wave with knives in it. My mind raced backward: the divorce, the silence, the distance I’d let grow between us like a wall I was too tired to climb. I’d been drowning in work, in fame, in pressure, in sickness,God, the sickness,and she’d been carrying this alone? Carrying her alone? My chest locked up completely. If I wasn’t already leaning against the pillows, I would’ve collapsed. My breath stuttered, harsh and painful, as if my lungs were made of gravel. Leo placed a hand on my arm, like he thought I’d pass out. “Isaiah. Hey. Breathe, okay? Slow, slow.” But slow wasn’t an option. Nothing about this moment was slow. Everything was hitting me too fast,like the universe had waited for the exact second my body was at its weakest to drop the heaviest truth of my life onto my chest. “I have… a daughter,” I said, the words tasting foreign and electric and devastating. “Leo, I have a daughter.” The sentence shattered me. It felt unreal, surreal, impossible,except it wasn’t. She was right there on the screen. Real. Alive. Two years old. Two years of first laughs, first steps, first words… Two years I missed. Two years I didn’t know. A tremor started in my hands and spread through my arms, my chest, my spine. Leo saw it instantly. “Isaiah, relax. Hey. You’re going to trigger the spasms again—” “I missed everything,” I choked out. “Her whole life. Leo—Alyssa never told me. She didn’t tell me. Why didn’t she tell me?” Leo didn’t answer. Maybe he couldn’t. The picture was still glowing from his phone. The little girl was looking into the camera with a half-smile, her green eyes cutting straight through me. God, she looked like me. Down to the exact shade. Down to the tiny stubborn tilt of her chin. “She’s mine,” I whispered, voice breaking in half. “I—I know she is. That’s my child.” Leo inhaled sharply but didn’t disagree. How could he? The proof was staring both of us down. And that’s when the panic hit full force. Not the frantic kind. Not the loud kind. The deep kind. The crushing kind. The kind that steals the air from your lungs and leaves nothing but ache and regret behind. My breath shortened. My chest tightened. The room spun slightly, tilting like a sinking ship. Not now, I begged my own body. Not now, not now,please not now. Leo moved fast, adjusting the oxygen tubes near my bed. “Isaiah, look at me. Breathe through your nose. Slow it down. Stay with me.” But I could barely hear him. All I could see was her. A little girl who didn’t know her father existed. A little girl I had never held. Never kissed. Never protected. A little girl who might grow up without me if this cancer kept spreading. My vision blurred again,tears or dizziness, I couldn’t tell. Probably both. “Why didn’t she tell me?” I whispered again, voice small, broken, afraid. “Leo… why didn’t Alyssa tell me?” Leo hesitated, then spoke gently, “Maybe she thought you wouldn’t want the child. Maybe she was protecting herself. Maybe she didn’t want a scandal. Maybe… she was just hurt.” I shook my head violently. “No. No, Leo,I should’ve known. I should’ve been there. I should’ve…” My voice faltered, collapsed. “I should’ve protected them.” He squeezed my arm. “You didn’t know, Zay.” “But I should have,” I said again, softer now, a whisper soaked in regret. I leaned back slowly, letting my head hit the pillow because I couldn’t hold myself up anymore. The nausea was back. The tremors were worse. And the ache spreading through my chest was nothing chemo could explain. But under all the shock and panic and heartbreak, something else flickered,weak but stubborn. A spark. A promise forming in the middle of the chaos. My daughter exists. And I will not leave this world without knowing her. I stared at the screen again, my breath finally evening out. Somewhere deep inside my exhausted, failing body… resolve settled in my bones. I didn’t know her name. I didn’t know her voice. I didn’t know what she liked, what she laughed at, what she was afraid of. But I knew one thing with absolute certainty: That little girl was mine. And I was going to fight for the chance to be her father,even if it killed me. Thirty As I expected, I received a message , a formal note, through Dad, who had flown in from LA with Mom the day after the Incident. When he went back to LA, he was greeted at the door by a letter from Isaiah’s lawyer. It didn’t “begin,” really. It demanded. It demanded that I schedule a formal meeting with Isaiah’s team. Not Isaiah himself , because God forbid the man actually act like a father or a human being , but his team. And that team wanted a paternity test. After all these years, he was still the same pathetic coward being puppeteered by people who only cared about his image. And the fact that Julian and Leo were the ones who contacted me? Not Isaiah? It made my blood boil. I told Dad to tell them I declined the meeting. My daughter is mine. Alone. Period. I have been silent enough. I have been used enough. For ten years of marriage, I let them control me because I didn’t want to ruin his reputation. But not anymore. Now I am my own person, and I’ll protect my daughter from their hungry eyes. Ray won’t be paraded as some PR miracle baby. That was two weeks ago. They haven’t said anything since. Good. But peace hasn’t existed in my world since Ray’s identity went public.
